speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN MOUNTED POLICE AND NATIONAL DEFENCE RESPECTING FORMER OFFICER
speechtext:
The other day in the course of the army estimates the hon. member for Lake Centre asked me to produce any correspondence which might have passed between the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Department of National Defence relating to one Mr. Elliott, a former officer in the army. I told him that if there were any letters which were properly producible, I would see that they were produced. My statement in that respect appears at page 5264 of Hansard, where I said:
If there is correspondence between the Royal Canadian Mounted Police which I take it is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice, and the Department of National Defence which is properly producible under the order, it -will be produced. If there is

Supply-Trade and Commerce
such correspondence, I do not know why it was not produced. I will look over the files, and if there is correspondence that is producible under that order, I will see that it is produced.
Mr. Diefenbaker: Without any qualification?
Mr. Abbott: Without qualification.
I find that I was in error in my assumption that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is under the Department of Justice. The order calls for the production of correspondence between the Department of National Defence, the Department of Labour and the Department of Justice. There are five letters, three from the commissioner of the Roye! Canadian Mounted Police, and two I think from the deputy minister of national defence in reply to these letters. All the letters are marked '*'confidential" and are not producible under the order. Of course, even if the order did call for the production of such correspondence it would not cover the confidential letters; therefore the letters cannot be produced.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN MOUNTED POLICE AND NATIONAL DEFENCE RESPECTING FORMER OFFICER
speechtext: Will the minister please tell us why there are so many objections to giving the full facts in connection with this matter-because one letter after another has been refused production? The minister now raises another question of confidential letters.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN MOUNTED POLICE AND NATIONAL DEFENCE RESPECTING FORMER OFFICER
speechtext: I did not raise the question of confidential letters, if my hon. friend will permit me. I raised the point that the order of the house does not call for the production of these letters. The letters are letters which passed between the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the deputy minister of national defence. No order of the house would have been passed calling for the production of such letters, and no order was passed. That is the ground on which I say that the letters are not producible. In addition, I mentioned that they are marked "confidential." I do not think it has ever been the practice of the house to require the production of letters from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in connection with their proceedings.

subtopic: CONDITIONS IN GLACE BAY AREA-MEAT RATIONING

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
^ Mr. CLARENCE GILLIS (Cape Breton South): I should like to direct a question to the Acting Minister of Finance. I did not have the opportunity of sending him notice of this question, because it arises out of a telegram I received this morning from the Retail Merchants Association of Glace Bay, Nova Scotia. Is there a possibility of relieving the extreme shortage of shortening and lard in that area? The merchants claim that they are receiving only fifty per cent of the supplies they were receiving in 1945. There is also a serious shortage of paper bags and wrapping paper. The merchants say that they have to discontinue the handling of a large number of commodities because of the shortage. These merchants question whether it is necessary to continue meat rationing. Will the minister take note of these questions and give me an answer when he can? I would appreciate his doing this.

subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON AUGUST 29

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): In the course of the discussion of the trade and commerce estimates yesterday an hon. member is reported at page 5608 of Hansard as having called me a mountebank. I will call him an angel, and both of us will be mistaken.
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

Canadian government travel bureau-
390. To assist in promoting tourist business in Canada, $650,000.

What coordination is there between the dominion and the provinces in advertising the tourist business? My riding is extremely interested in the tourist trade and the Ontario government is doing a good deal to that end. I should like to know something about the coordination between the two governments
561S
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: The tourist branch of the department realizes the importance of the closest cooperation with the various tourist agencies in the provinces and tries to maintain the closest contact with them. As Minister of Trade and Commerce I have called a meeting for Ottawa for the month of October, and all the provincial ministers in charge of the tourist business have responded one hundred per cent. In each case they have stated that they heartily approve our plans for coordination and have assured us that they will be present with their officials.

That seems wise and right. In what has actually been done up to the moment, has there been any consultation with the provinces? Take Ontario, for example. Have there been any conversations with the Ontario department?

I understand the
director of this department maintains close contact with similar organizations doing this work not only in Ontario but in the other provinces.

This morning I received a letter from the secretary of the Alberta boards cf trade. This organization coordinates the work of all the boards of trade of the province. The letter urged me to press for action in respect to the building of landing strips for tourists coming into the country. I know that this is not directly under the minister's department, but the letter suggested that air strips should be built at such places as Banff and Lake Louise. I do not know whether there would be any place at Lake Louise, because it is mountainous, but the suggestion would apply to Jasper and other parks. A good deal of the tourist traffic in the future will be earned by air. I call this to the attention of the minister because it might be discussed at the future conference. I would ask him to take the matter up with his colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources and canvass the possibilities in that direction, because it deserves consideration.
It does deserve the closest attention and support, and I am in close touch with it. I shall be glad to carry out the hon. gentleman's suggestion.

I would remind the minister that in March last I pointed out to him that in the advertising of the tourist business, so far as maps are concerned, Prince Edward Island appeared to be entirely omitted. He kindly stated that he would give the matter

his attention. I would once more remind him of it and ask him to make a note of this so that our province will not be left out again.

The information that I had was that the map in question was not the product of any Canadian department of government or any Canadian institution, but was published by private individuals in the United States. I believe I pointed that out to the hon. member on a former occasion. However, I will make a note of the question.

The map which the tourist bureau sends to Americans giving information about Canada does not show this country to good advantage. Accompanying the map should be a letter informing the recipients that maps of various sections would be sent to them. I also suggest that w'hen the conference is held the provinces be asked to indicate on their maps the different highways to available camping sites, because many Americans come here in trailers with camp equipment and go hundreds of miles without being able to find a camp.

Item agreed to.
Foreign trade services-
S61. Trade publicity and advertising in Canada and abroad-further amount required, $16,750.

I have some questions on the order paper respecting the export of lumber. How does the minister's department ascertain whether any company is shipping more than fifty per cent of its lumber? My information respecting one company is that it is shipping practically one hundred per cent of the lumber it produces, and ignores representations made to it by the Department of Trade and Commerce.

The operations to which the hon. member has referred are under the direction of the timber controller, in another department of government. However he maintains a close check, and it would be difficult for me to believe that any one company is allowed to ship anything like its total production, or a quantity which would be out of line with the amount shipped by other companies seeking the export field.

That may be so, but I should like to have some factual information on it. As the minister will have observed from my questions on the order paper, this company is also a producer of pulp and paper. All the lumber produced is of first-class quality, the poorer parts going into the pulp and

Supply-Trade and Commerce
paper mill. The people in Vancouver are having great difficulty in obtaining first-class lumber, my information being that the lumber offered for sale is of third or perhaps fourth quality, and that that is all that is left for the smaller dealers. It may be that we have already dealt with the item respecting the timber controller. I suggest however, that this matter should be checked further so that British Columbia builders may have at least a fair share of the lumber produced in that province.

Item agreed to.
8G3. Electricity and gas inspection services, including administration of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act-further amount required, $46,720.

I should like to ask a question respecting the checking of weights and measures. My understanding is that inspectors are appointed to check weights and measures throughout the country, for which they charge a fee. For instance, when a check is made on gasoline pumps a fee is charged for each pump. What is the revenue derived from these fees?
This item was passed yesterday but I shall be glad to get the information and let the hon. member have it later to-day.

If an operator has three or four pumps it costs him S15 or S20 every time an inspector comes around. That inspector can check perhaps eight or ten places each day, and it would seem to me the fees charged would bring in considerable revenue. Yet this department asks for about $1,800,000 for the purpose. Would the revenue not cover the costa in the department?
This is a self-supporting service, the fees taking care of the expenses. The revenue goes into the consolidated revenue fund ffbcount.

These inspectors when checking scales use weights running up to 500 pounds. I have in mind an instance in which scales were checked, but after several years it was found that because of wear in the scales, when a weight passed over them, near the weighing capacity of the scale, the mechanism would lower to the point that it was resting on the foundation. The weights were entirely wrong; yet these people had paid over a number of years for having the scales checked. When inspectors check the scales I suggest they should use a weight equalling the capacity of the scale, if they wish to ascertain whether or not the scale is operating efficiently.
In the instance I have in mind it cost several hundred dollars to have the necessary repairs made, and it was the weighman who found the mistake. This scale would probably weigh a load from ten to twelve tons, but the check would be made with a weight of only 100 or 200 pounds. This does not give a true indication of the weighing capacity of the scale.
I shall see that that is brought to the attention of the department.

When item S61 was called, owing to the fact that we were proceeding rapidty I did not have an opportunity to ask a question I had in mind. I notice that this vote asks for a further amount of $16,750, although we have already passed an item of $459,000 for the same thing. While I do not object to these amounts, I would ask the minister to .tell me w'hat proportion of the money is to be spent on advertising in Canada. I have read carefully some of the advertisements issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce and published in Canadian periodicals, and I must confess that I have never been able to see the sense in advertising our foreign trade to our own people. They are more interested in buying Canadian products than in being fed with propaganda to bolster a foreign trade mania. I can see no other purpose in this advertising than that of trying to influence the minds of the people with the thought that the present Liberal administration is attempting to do the right thing by pursuing this particular policy. It may be the right thing; but I claim there is at least an element of using the taxpayers money to support a particular policy. I am certain if I were to take the time to read one of these advertisements and to question the minister upon it, it would cause him some embarrassment. I am not going to do that, but I would ask what proportion of these amounts, now totalling about $476,000, is spent for advertising in Canada. If the minister cannot give me the information now, I shall be content to receive it later.
I will do that.
I take it we are still discussing the main item covering foreign trade services?
Item 863.

That is only one of the items under foreign trade services. Are we not discussing the general item of foreign trade services and then the details under item 863?
Supply-Trade and Commerce
This item deals with electricity and gas inspection services.

There were some matters I desired to discuss under foreign trade in general, and I suppose it will be in order to discuss them now, because we are dealing with the general item of foreign trade services. , I should like to ask a question or two as to what is Canada's ultimate objective with respect to trade, why she wishes to attain that objective, and whether she is giving any consideration to the probable international disharmony which may result from attaining it. I think matters of this kind should be considered for a few minutes, but if you rule against me I shall have to desist.
We shall have to deal with the specific item. There was a general discussion on administration, but we are now dealing with a specific item.

Item agreed to.
Dominion bureau of statistics-
86-J. Administration - further amount required, $5,810.

I should like to revert back to item 862. You are proceeding pretty fast; I do not object to that, but when you do I should not like to be denied the right to go back to some of the items that have been passed. Item 862 deals with the wheat and grain division, I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to a matter that was raised yesterday, the meeting in Washington of the preparatory committee of the international wheat council. The minister knows and the committee will remember that we now have a wheat agreement with the United Kingdom for a period of five years. In answer to a question I asked yesterday the minister intimated that an official of his department, Mr. Wilson, was now in Washington attending the preparatory committee of the international wheat council. I asked the miinster if he could tell us anything as to what was going on, and he said that he did not feel that he could. In view of the agreement which has been made with Britain and the discussions now proceeding, in Washington, can the minister not tell us something more about what policies are being advanced by our officials in Washington? Under the United Kingdom agreement this country has arranged to sell two-thirds of its wheat crop for a period of four or five years, and we now have an official in Washington talking with other nations about some other plans for wheat. Will the minister tell us whatever he can as to what is going on and what position our representative is taking before that committee?

As I stated to the committee yesterday or the day before, the international wheat conference has been in session on and off for several years, in an effort to bring forward definite recommendations which can be made to the various governments represented at the conference to regulate the supply and price of wheat internationally. The countries represented there are the importing and exporting countries. I think it would be inadvisable at the present time for me to say just what are the bases of the conversations, but the representatives of the various countries are endeavouring to arrive at some international arrangement that can be recommended to the countries they represent.

Can the minister be a little more specific? The government is sending officials to Washington, and they cannot be going without some instructions. Are they just sent there and told to sit down with the other people to talk things over and then come back and tell what they hear? Or are they sent there with some definite instructions or objectives in mind? I do not want- to embarrass the minister, but this is an important matter affecting one of the major sections of the Canadian economy. With parliament in session the government has somebody down there dealing with our whole economy. Some action may be taken and decided upon before this house or the Canadian people even know what is going on. I would like the minister to tell us what he feels he can as to what instructions this official was given when he went to this meeting.

The wheat committee of the cabinet are In frequent consultation with the present representative, the ch^rman of the Canadian wheat board, who also attends these meetings, and another official of ours at Washington. The progress of the discussion is reported to us and suggestions are made. It is inadvisable for me to say rnoj-e than I have said. An effort is being made by the representatives of the various nations to reach some conclusion which they can recommend to their respective governments on the matter of international wheat prices. I do not think I can say anything else, and I want the hon. member to understand that I am not trying to hold back anything.

Is it not correct that three or four years ago several countries agreed on a tentative international wheat agreement?

___________ Supply-Trade and Commerce
That is the foundation of these present meetings.

An agreement was arrived at which was to be carried out immediately on the termination of the war, but something has happened. Can the minister tell us why there has been delay in proceeding with these plans as originally contemplated?

Meetings have been held from time to time and adjourned because of differences of opinion. An effort is being made to bring the countries to a common understanding. The reason for delay is simply the inability to bring the different countries to some common understanding or agreement.
Then your representative is seeking to bring about something like what was proposed in the international wheat agreement of three or four years ago?
He has no authority to bind this government, but he has instructions to continue discussions along that line.
Are the government elevators at the head of the lakes still being leased, and if so, to whom, and what is the term of the lease and the amount involved?

Yesterday I had one of the members of the board of Grain Commissioners here with me just for the purpose of assisting me in answering such questions, but when the item was passed yesterday this supplementary was overlooked and I think the official went home last night.
What company is leasing the elevators?
We called for tenders some months ago for leasing the elevator, and the only tender we received was from McCabe Brothers.
They had it before.

Yes. The tender was not altogether satisfactory to us, and we negotiated with them and got a little better arrangement. Their tender was the only one, and the elevator is now under lease to McCabe Brothers.
At what price?
I have not that before me, but I shall be glad to get it for my hon. friend.

One other question in regard to the matter I raised a few moments ago with regard to the tentative international wheat agreement which was proposed three or four years ago-five years ago, I am told.
Can the minister now say whether that pro-_ posed agreement had the approval of this ' government, I rather thought it had, but I am not sure-or was it just a proposal that was advanced by officials of different governments?

Any reply I make on that is subject to correction, because I am speaking from memory. I do not remember any formal approval by this government of the result of the negotiations referred to. If there is some specific point on which my hon. friend wants information, I shall endeavour to give it to him.

My question is specific. I am asking, did this government approve the proposed international wheat agreement which was arranged in 1942, I think it was, by several governments? The minister said a little while ago that the officials had no power to bind the government, which everybody recognizes. But here was an agreement proposed and talked about as something good for the future, and I am asking whether it had the endorsa-tion or approval of this government. The minister does not need to answer now, but I should like an answer before the house adj ourns.

I might as well answer now. I have no recollection of any formal ratification or adoption by this government of any arrangement made by the delegates at the international wheat conference. It is the w'ish of the government, though, that an agreement be reached between the exporting and importing companies that will guarantee the wheat economy of Canada.
Will the minister say whether or not that arrangement had the endorsement of this government?
I have just answered that.
No, the minister said that he had no recollection of it.

I am not trying to split hairs or avoid answering. I am telling the hon. member the exact truth. I have no recollection of that having been done. I do not think there was any formal acceptance by this government of any international wheat agreement or of the recommendations that were made, but I do not want to be too positive about it.

Is not that question capable of a definite answer? Can the minister not look back over his records and then state

Supply-Trade and Commerce

definitely whether the agreement proposed wa3 approved by the government or not? He has told us that he is speaking from memory, but surely he can ascertain definitely whether the agreement was approved by this government or not. I do not want to embarrass the minister, but I should like to have an answer later.

Item agreed to.
Dominion bureau of statistics-
865.	Statistics - further amount required, 1196,718.

This further amount of S1E6,71S is in addition to the main vote we passed last night of 82,090,670 for statistics for 1946-47. Why does the minister find it necessary to ask for this further amount in ad*-dition to the large vote we passed for statistics last night, and which in itself was an increase of $4S2,070 over the previous year? Why was not this 8196,718 included in the main estimates tabled some months ago?

The main estimates were prepared towards the end of October last, many months ago. The increase is largely accounted for by an item of $129,488 which the bureau of statistics requires for the preparation of an index of deaths as of January 1, 1925 to date and continuing.
Did the minister not know last fall that this work was required to be done?

No, the Department of Health and Welfare came to us comparatively recently and told us that they have found it necessary to have this index of deaths for checking purposes in connection with the family allowance.

Item agreed to.
Dominion bureau of statistics-
866.	Census of population-further amount required, $86,680.

I notice that SS6.6S0 is the further amount required in addition to the SI,2.19,685 that we passed in item 382 in the main estimates for a census of population, making a total of $1,306,365. Is a census to be taken of the population this year?

The quinquennial
census for the three western provinces is under way now. That census has to be taken in accordance with the agreement made when these provinces were formed.
Is this amount and the amount voted last year in connection with the census all required for the census in the three western provinces?
That is correct.
It is not for any other part of Canada?
No, just the three western provinces.

Last April I asked the names and addresses of the census commissioners in the three prairie provinces, which information I received. I asked also which of these are veterans of the first and second world wars. That question was not answered, but a note was added that the information was obtainable. I think I brought the matter to the minister's attention once since then. Has he the information now?

I directed the officials of the bureau of statistics in charge of this census by circular letter to the census commissioners to obtain this information. The following memo was given to me. It is not a direct answer to the question, but I will give it as I have received it from the officials of the department.
The census commissioners must be carefully selected because of the importance of the work in their charge. Special qualifications are required. If the commissioners are well known and have numerous contacts, it facilitates the carrying out of the census, as people object to giving some information to enumerators. The right kind of commissioner can smooth out such difficulties. In consequence most of our commissioners appointed for the western census are men of quite mature years. There are fifty-six in all, thirty-three of whom are over fifty years of age, and eight between forty and fifty. A considerable number have been commissioners in previous censuses. Eleven of these men have had overseas service, seven of them in the first world war and four in the last. In addition, four served in Canada. Four were physically unfit and unable to take part in the war activities.
May I ask whether, when the census takes place in 1950, the western provinces will be again included, or will the census taken for this year stand until 1956?

Yes; the three western provinces will be included in the next dominion census. This special census is taken for a variety of reasons. The main one, I think, is that upon it is based the amount of money given to each of these three provinces by the dominion government in lieu of other considerations.

Supply-Trade and. Commerce
How are these census commissioners appointed? Is it through the civil service commission, or a matter of direct appointment by the department?
These men are not appointed by the civil service commission. They are appointed by the department, or really by the minister in charge.

Is it the policy of the department in appointments of this type to give preference to veterans of the first or the second world war? I imagine that that would be the policy, but apparently in this case it was not, because it was not even known in the first place when I asked this question which of them were veterans and which were not, so apparently there was no thought of giving any preference to veterans. I have further proof of that by checking up from the local branch of the Canadian Legion at Dauphin, asking them if they had been consulted on this appointment in the Dauphin district. Their reply, dated June 17 and signed by the secretary of the branch, is that they had not been consulted in any way in the appointment of the census commissioner for that district. I do not want to kick up too much of a dust about it at this time,, because the thing is over; the census has been taken; it is a dead horse. But I do wish to lodge a protest. Here is one case in which the local branches should have been consulted and I think could have recommended to the minister suitable men who were veterans. To my knowledge there are men in the Dauphin district who could have served very well in that position. But the legion was not consulted, and in looking over the list I received in answer to question No.
1 I am inclined to suspect-I would not make this as a categorical statement-that the appointments seem to follow more or less of a patronage trend. The minister can say whether that is so or not.
That would be an accident !

He said a moment ago that appointments are made of men who have "wide contacts" within the district. I must say that in Winnipeg North, for example, the gentleman who was appointed happened to be the defeated Liberal candidate-who, I imagine has fairly good contacts.
I imagine he would have.

Although experience
showed, as an hon. friend suggests, that his contacts were not sufficient.
He didn't make the best use of what he did contact.
He just didn't have enough.

I find other instances of defeated candidates of the. Liberal party or other good wheel-horses who did very good work for the Liberal candidate. I do not want to mention any names, but that has happened close to my own district. I want to tell the minister, while I have the opportunity, for his own information that there is a considerable amount of resentment amongst veterans who feel that they should have been consulted and should have had an opportunity of recommending men for these positions, because the men are available, men who served in the first great war and in the second great war, who could have done that job just as well, and to whom, I believe, the preference to which they were entitled should have been extended.

I would like to support what the hon. member has said, in the line of reasoning with the minister-and we believe he is a man one can reason with-that it does not tend to the credit of the government to have that sort of thing going on. While some of these men have done good work and carried out their job properly, the fact of the matter is that the way they were appointed leaves that stigma.
A moment ago, when the minister was replying to a question of the hon. member for New Westminster he explained that the five year censuses in the prairie provinces are necessary in order to determine payments of subsidies due to those provinces. I should like to follow that up a little farther.
Don't go too far.
Never mind; that is what we are here for, to go on to the proper conclusion, to get the proper answers.
No; he is here to go home.

It is quite proper to go
home when the work is done. I should like the minister to give the information, if it is available, as to just what benefit this has been in past years to these provinces or to the dominion government. I can understand that in the beginning, when the provinces were first organized and tremendous increases of population were taking place for a few years, these censuses were necessary. But is it worth while, now, after this period of time, to have a census every five years, and what action does the government take in respect to increases
Supply[DOT]-Trade and Commerce

or decreases in population in that period? For instance, if we have a redistribution bill passed at the next session-and it might have been passed this session-it would not take into consideration any decided increase that we might have in Saskatchewan, but would still use the 1940 census as the basis, with the result that so far as the redistribution is concerned the census would not amount to anything to any of the three western provinces.
I should like to know from the minister if the census at the present time every five years is worth while, or should steps be taken to make some arrangement with the provinces which we can get on the ordinary basis. I am not suggesting that we should; but I should like to know just what advantage has accrued to the provinces or to the dominion by having these censuses. .

The taking of this census is a statutory requirement. I am told that in 1936 there was a suggestion that this quinquennial census be dropped. But it was retained, not only because it is a statutory obligation but because of the strong demands from the three western provinces for its continuance. Redistribution is based on the ten year census, not on the quinquennial.
I am not saying it should be done away with, but I should like to know what the three prairie provinces have gained from the quinquennial census.
I have not the figures in front of me; I can get them for my hon. friend.
I have been informed that the census commissioner for Yorkton is the president of the Liberal association. Does the minister know whether that is true or not?
I do not know whether it is true, but quite possibly it is true.
Thank you very much.

I can tell the hon. member that I listened carefully to the representations made by the hon. member for Dauphin, but in spite of that I have not had one single criticism from my province or from any other part of Canada as to the manner in which the census commissioners have carried on their work.

Since the minister has made that remark I want to make it clear that I am not complaining about the manner in which they are doing their work. I imagine that they do their work efficiently. I was complaining about the manner in which they were being appointed, because it smacks of political patronage, and I object to that.
 *
Mail subsidies and steamship subventions-Eastern local services-
870. Grand Manan and the mainland, service between-further amount required, $52,000.
Halifax, Canso and Guysboro, service between -further amount required, $16,000.
Owen Sound and ports on Manitoulin island and Georgian bay, service between-further amount required, $30,000.
Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, service between-further amount required, $45,000.
Saint John, Westport and Yarmouth and other way ports, service between-further amount required, $7,000.
There is an amount in this item for the Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia service on the Wood islands route, where there are two steamers.
Yes.

The Prince Nova and the Charles A. Dunning; this service given by the Northumberland ferries is the very best service that we have with the mainland. They are giving a service to-day which is beneficial to the farmers, because their rates on automobiles and trucks with freight are common sense rates and not an overcharge in any way to be compared with those in effect on the Borden-Tormentine ferries. The rate is hardly more than one-third of that which is charged on the Canadian National Railway on the Borden-Tormentine ferry. Is that the limit that the minister is going to give to the Northumberland ferries for that excellent service. I suppose they have made representations to him. If they are satisfied with it I am glad to see it in the estimates this year.
Item agreed to. '

Customs and excise divisions-
247. General administration, $1,040,595.
Will the minister tell us why there is an increase this year.

Will it be possible to reconsider the imposing of taxes on community groups which are organized for the chief purpose of developing the musical abilities of the individual boys and girls and young people in a community? I have particular reference to a group known as the Alcan Follies. The primary object of this group is not to provide entertainment but to educate boys and girls. To this end they have spent a good deal of their money to form their organization and get their instruments, music and so forth. We are at a loss to know why music festivals should not be taxed-and I do not think they should be'-whereas organizations of this kind are. Will the minister promise to give reconsideration to this point? I have already discussed it with him privately, and I should like him to express an opinion on the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
The matter as it stands is that where an amusement of the type referred to is entirely for charitable purposes the amusement tax is not collected; but where part of the benefits accrue to an individual or to a group of individuals, the amusement tax is applied. Where they are strictly charitable and for purposes'that have been indicated by the hon. member, and where the money which is received does not accrue either to an individual or to a group of individuals, the tax is not collected. Further consideration might be given to what the hon. member suggests.

I should like to get some information on a question I brought up under other departments. Probably I can get it in this department. In the exporting of goods to the United States, to what are called the free port zones, the customs department in Charlottetown last year did not seem to have any information whatever as to how to proceed with shipments. I recall one case in which a man came into the province with the intention of exporting a considerable quantity of goods. He was buying and exporting goods to the free port zone in New York, and the customs officer at Charlottetown, properly so, took the matter up on this man's behalf with Ottawa, but it took a whole day before the exporter could get his papers through. What I am coming at is this. The department should provide these customs officers with all the necessary information for shipments of that kind. I realize that such shipments are new; that is, shipping dutiable goods into a country and placing them in the so-called free port zones. They do not pay the duty until the article is sold. I would ask the minister to give instructions to our customs agents and other men in similar positions so that too much trouble will not be caused the exporter. The department has a customs officer in Charlottetown who cannot be surpassed for service to the people. I believe he extracts every cent of duty it is possible to get on an article but he takes it by the painless method. I do not believe there is any man in the customs department in any province who is held in higher esteem than Mr. Goodwin, and I am glad to say this on his behalf, because he did excellent work on the occasion I speak of. He used the telephone and telegraph, he got in touch with New York and Ottawa, and as I say, it took a day for the man to get his papers completed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
What sort of commodity
was he dealing in?

Furs. They were dutiable and were going into the free zone.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: The free zone would not make so much difference. Our department acts as agent for trade and commerce, and if the shipper had the proper export permit there would be no delay on our part. I am glad to hear the commendation of the officer at Charlottetown, and I may say that similar comments come from one end of the country to the other with regard to the service of all the officers.

The express company should know that the article is dutiable and that the ordinary export entry is not sufficient. If they knew this they would not carry the article. I suggest that instructions be given the officer down there when he issues the export permit so as to have it acceptable to the express company or whatever transport company it may be.

Is it the policy of the government now to reopen some of the ports of entry from the United States which were closed during the. depression years? Conditions have changed since that time, and the reopening of these ports would not only facilitate tourist traffic coming into Canada but would in the long run be a good thing for our economy, because it would make it easier for our own people to move back and forth between this country and the. United States and it would provide a certain number of veterans with employment, because at many of these ports of entry we have veterans who are doing an excellent job. I have in mind a certain port of entry in Saskatchewan which I know very well and which was closed. It is south of Weyburn at a place called Beaubier, which was closed in the depression years. There is a considerable demand that that port be reopened so as to facilitate traffic between the United States and Canada. The minister will no doubt say that when the traffic justifies the reopening of the port it will be reopened, but I would point out that there is no way of gauging what the traffic is, because many of these people go to other ports of entry and have to go many miles out of their way in order to move back and forth. Has there been any change of policy in relation to these ports?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: It is not contemplated that there will be any change in the policy with reference to the opening of ports that have been closed. As a result of an investigation by a royal commission some years ago the recommendation was made that many of these smaller ports be closed with a view to improving the appraisal system. We have found that sufficient service is being given all along the border line, and that service is improved because of the fact that we are able to get men who are: better fitted to make, the appraisal. It has been a matter of economy, without diminishing the service, rendered the country.

In the budget speech last autumn the Minister of Finance said he realized there was a great deal of questioning in the country not only as to the taxation law, not only as to the amount of taxation fixed, but. as to the procedure, the machinery of collection. He said at that time, if I remember correctly, that he was proposing to see that a full inquiry and review into the whole situation was made. I am not so sure he referred to it specifically in his last speech, but I believe there: was a reference there, and I should like to know what has been done and is being done. Anyone will agree it is a matter of common knowledge that people throughout Canada are greatly troubled about the various aspects of the machinery and procedure, and have been longing for simplifications.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
I believe I can assure the hon. member that the matter is well in hand. The Minister of Finance in his budget speech said, I believe, that a departmental committee had been set up, and that the legislation is

Supply-Revenue-Taxation
now under review. The matter of administration was canvassed by a committee which worked on it for some time and presented a report which I tabled in the house at the last session, early in December. That had to do with the establishment of adidtional district offices in Canada. It is proposed almost to double the number of offices at present in operation. In adition to the main office in Ottawa we have nineteen regional offices, and it is proposed to add thirteen, bringing the total to thirty-three. Because of the scarcity of materials for construction we are having some difficulty in getting available accommodation in towns and cities in which we intend to open these additional offices. The Department of Public Works has had difficulty in doing any building. It rs equally difficult to lease premises. Then there is the matter of personnel. It is difficult to get a sufficient number of people with training as auditors or assessors or in other skills necessary in connection with income tax and succession duties. However this whole matter is under review, and progress is being made toward the objective we have in mind, "that of giving better service to the public.

The minister's statement seems both satisfactory and unsatisfactory. As to having more local offices and extending facilities, I should think that would be a wise procedure. I had not expressed any opinion on that, but it sounds reasonable. What I wish still to know is this. Is there any basic revision-and this is what the Minister of Finance suggested last autumn-or is the department just ironing out little inequalities which might occur here and there? My impression is that the last time this matter was considered, and when it was discussed in the press, the view was that it went very deep. It was not simply a matter of adding a few offices here and there, but rather one of going to the very root of our taxation procedure. Probably that is difficult at the present time, owing to changing conditions. But has there been a basic study, not of this or that detail in connection with offices or personnel, but of the whole taxation structure? I am not referring only to a routine review, because I know it is always being subjected to that. I want to know whether a basic review is being made, because nothing less than that was contemplated in the minister's remarks last October.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
I think if the hon. member will review what was said by the Minister of Finance he will see that the basic review has to do with the legislative side of the matter. That is being studied. What I referred to
more practicularly, and what I know more about, is the administration end of it. Progress is being made along that line. It is being studied from the legislative point of view, and ultimately will be reviewed.

The minister said he was going to open new offices; I hope one of them will be at Peterborough, because we certainly need one. While I am on my feet I should like to ask about inspection of income tax. The department sends inspectors to different offices. I have in mind an instance in which two inspectors went into an office while the man in charge was busy. They said, "We would like to see your books." He said, "I am busy, but you are welcome to them. Come into my inner office and I shall get them for you." He seated them at a desk, got his books, placed them on the desk and said, "Gentlemen, if there is anything further, just call me and I shall come out and check it with you." He was busy for some time, and upon returning to the office discovered that the inspectors had gone. They had gone through his books- and had also gone through his desk and taken a few odds and ends out of it, without his knowledge. I do not think that is proper procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: I agree with the hon. member, one hundred per cent. That was malfeasance of office, and will not be condoned.
I am glad to hear that, because I did not think the minister would stand for it.

I was pleased to hear that the minister is considering the opening of more regional offices. Last winter I had occasion to meet a number of farmers in my constituency who were going to the regional office in Saskatoon. They had to travel three hundred miles, and it took them four days. If there were more regional offices I believe the department would get more funds and the farmers would get more satisfaction. I met these men when they were returning from Saskatoon, and they felt that they had received satisfaction from having travelled to that office. Some of the difficulties which had been troubling them were ironed out. They did not hare to pay as much as they thought they would have to pay. When the minister is considering these new regional offices I hope he will put one in North Battleford. If he needs any help in securing a building, I shall be glad to cooperate with him.

I do not believe the setting up of more regional offices will remedy the situation. I do hope that the new legisla-
Supply-Revenue-Taxation

tion being considered in connection with the collection of income tax will put that collection on a businesslike basis. There is nothing more inadequate than the present method of collecting income tax. It would be against the law for any private business to penalize a person for not paying a bill which had been rendered. In my opinion a taxpayer should submit what he considers is an honest return on his income during a certain year, and the government in turn should render a bill, and until such time as the government has rendered the bill, there should be no penalty. A private concern could not do it, and it is ridiculous for the government to impose a penalty in connection with income tax returns that are not made out correctly, probably through no fault of the persons concerned. This is especially so when the department itself is two or three years behind in checking returns. -

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: There is no law that requires anyone to send a bill.
You know what I mean.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: A notice of assessment is not a bill, it is statutory; it must be in by April 30 of the succeeding year for which a return is made. In essence that is the bill. The man makes out his own bill, which is examined and corrected and then the assessment notice is sent out.
Does the minister consider it right that a man should be penalized when the department is three years behind?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: As a matter of equity any man who owes money to the crown for three years should not have the use of that money without paying for it.
Yes, but he is not aware that he owes the money to the crown until three years after he is supposed to have paid it.

Has there been any improvement in the checking of income tax returns in order that a person may know before four or five years whether the return is correct or not? Perhaps there was some excuse duing the war for this delay, but in peace time the returns should be along before four or five years. As the hon. member for Wentworth has said, a man does not know whether his return is correct or not. Then when he is advised that there is an error and he owes the government so much money, he is charged interest and then on top of that a penalty is imposed. One case was brought to my attention in which a man was advised after three or four years that he owed money and that they would garnishee his wages if it was not

paid. He was able to show a marked cheque with which he had paid his income tax when it became due.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
The income tax officials are not infallible. You can pick out isolated cases in any business where errors occur. The matter of assessing is being much improved, but we cannot make the transition in the administration from war time to peace time as quickly as some people would like or as we would like. During the war years it was hard to get the proper type of official for the department, and as a result of that, and with the great increase in the number of returns during those years, there could not be anything but delay in making the assessments. We are on the road to bringing conditions back in conformity with normal business methods, and within a short time I think the public will see a considerable improvement.
There are some district offices in which the assessments are almost up to date for the preceding year. In the Ottawa office the assessments for 1944 are ninety-eight to ninety-nine per cent up to date, which is a good record. The 1945 return does not come in until the end of April, 1946; you have to have a period after that, and of necessity assessments are at least one year after the returns are made.

Does the minister think it fair that a man making a return which is correct to the best of his knowledge should have it sent back after a number of years with the statement that it is not correct and that he must pay a penalty? I cannot see any justice in that.

A few moments ago the minister answered me by saying that a person who owed the crown money should pay reasonable interest. I agree with him, but I support the hon. member for Durham who contends that he should not be penalized on top of having to pay the interest.

The minister may be correct in saying that legally a man who owes should pay interest; if he has calculated wrongly I suppose it is presumed to be his own fault and he should pay. However, the crown is not following its policy of extremely low interest rates, and I agree with hon. members who have spoken that if you charge a good round rate of interest, that ought to be enough.

Has consideration been given to increasing the exemption, if I may put it that way, allowed for a farmer's wife? I do not particularly like the word "exemption," but I

will have to use it. I know this matter comes under another department, but the administration is under the minister.
That would be under the Department of Finance.

Administration would be
under this department.
That does not come under National Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: As every one knows, the Department of National Revenue is entirely administrative. No matter what the rules or regulations are, we try to carry them out. If the hon. member wishes to have something changed, he should take it up with the Minister of Finance.

The minister did not answer my question. I asked him if he thought it fair that people should be penalized. Perhaps the Minister of Justice could give an opinion.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: As I understand it, there is no penalty. There is a statutory rate of interest charged up to thirty days after the notice of assessment is delivered to the taxpayer. It is only if he fails to pay within thirty days from the notice that there is an increase in the rate of interest. That increase is the only penalty I know of, unless there has been failure to comply with the requirements of the law in respect to the production of returns. As I understand it, the income tax is due on a certain date. A large number of the ratepayers are fortunate enough to be able to make out their returns in a manner that is not very much varied by the assessors when they go over the returns. Others, some no doubt in good faith and perhaps some who are not sure of their ground:, take the benefit of the doubt in their own favour in making up the statement of what they should pay. If it is found that they have made it up at too low an amount, there is a rate of interest charged to them from the due date to the thirtieth day after the delivery of the notice of assessment. That is supposed to be a rate of interest charged for their having had in the meantime the use of the money.

Eight per cent.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is four per cent up to thirty days after the taxpayer receives his notice of assessment. Then, if the amount shown in the assessment is not paid within the thirty days, the rate goes up to seven per cent. I do not know of any penalty other
than that additional two per cent which is the extra rate for not paying within the thirty days.

I have not a tax form with me, but I know I had to pay a penalty which was pretty near as much as the amount of the interest. I had no notification for three or four years after I made my return that it was not correct.
What interest is due the man who has overpaid his tax three or four years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: It is a long established rule and custom that the crown does not pay any interest.

I had an experience with a case that was sent to me this year which I think I should mention. I finally took it up with the deputy minister. In Toronto what wre need more than anything else is more space for the income tax office. The staff is very efficient, but you just cannot pile more and more people into a crowded office and expect results. The business of the office will be conducted far more efficiently if more space is provided for the people who have to work there. They are very much overcrowded. I compliment this staff on the work they are doing under such conditions. They are doing a real good job. The deputy knows the situation in Toronto, and I would ask the minister to take this matter under his wing and see if we cannot get more office space. Then wTe should need fewer people, they would all be happier, and a far better job would be done.

Item agreed to.

General-
256. Government office economies control division-administration, $10,910.

This is a very important item, and I would like to hear the minister say something about it. I would like to know the scope of this new office and what has been the experience of the men in it. What have they been able to do in the important matter they have to deal with?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
The	government office
economies control was established in 1942 to examine and review' all requisitions in the public service for printing, stationery, office equipment and furniture before purchases are made, and in general to apply the terms and regulations embodied in P.C. 4428 and amendments thereto. Administration is centred in the director, whose duty it is to determine the necessity for the articles requisitioned as also the quantity involved. While records are maintained showing the number of requisitions dealt with and estimated saving in each instance as a result of revision, any attempt to show by figures the economies effected in monetary value would not give the full amount, as no indication could be given of recurrent savings. In addition to screening requisitions received each day a careful review has been made of over 12,000 printed forms in use in the departments of the public service, and through substitution, lower grade quality of papers, standard size cut of forms, considerable initial and recurrent savings have been effected. All free mailing lists in the departments of government have been curtailed to a minimum. Standardization of qualities of paper in public printing and re-use of envelopes many times over have been effected, as well as reduction in qualities of binding of periodicals, publications, and so forth.
Careful review is made of all requisitions for publications, journals and other printed periodicals required for use of departments, and approval is confined to periodicals and scientific journals of use only to departments and libraries of government.
The teletype system in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply has been extended to all departments of government through the efforts of the division, and is widely used by numerous departments, with an annual estimated saving of approximately $80,000 on telegraphic accounts alone. The amount of savings resultant by elimination of long distance phone calls cannot be computated.
Periodic inspection is made of all government stores at Ottawa to ensure that stock

Supply-Revenue-Taxation
is properly shelved and kept in clean and good condition. Inspection is also made of duplicating sections of departments of government and examination made of qualities of papers used on duplicating machines; furtherance of single space and narrow margin on copy and elimination of waste of paper and inks, et cetera, maintained.
Careful scrutiny is given to requisitions for office machines and a number of transfers have been effected where machines are known to be surplus in any department.
A general tie-in has been made with this division acting as liaison between departments of government and War Assets Corporation for all office equipment declared surplus.
Considerable study has been given by the director to the advisability of having dormant records microfilmed so as to save the purchase of filing cabinets and space entailed in the filing and storage of dormant and semidormant files, and all departments have been advised accordingly. Several departments have adopted this process, and from information and records gathered it is believed that many other departments will follow.
I can give the duties of the director.
No. That is enough, thanks.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: I can give the hon. member some indication of the savings we have made.

I thank the minister, and I realize that I was wrong in my conception of the scope of the duty of this department. It is very much narrower than I realized. Perhaps I should have known that before. But it leads me to ask this question. At the time of the budget speech we on this side ventured to make some suggestions as to economy which the Minister of Finance, with unusual acerbity, said were very puny. The only thing I can say is that considering the actual economies which have been made they were like comparing a mountain with a mouse. I want to be realistic, and if possible even fair, and I know that reducing expenditures at this time is not easy. I know also that when you have a civil service of 150,000 it is difficult to know just where to begin, and I am equally convinced that unless there is somebody in a senior position who has the duty and the responsibility and the power, we need not expect any adequate reductions. I think we can also take it that when you have 150.000 people working, not all of them are working efficiently.
We all have the very greatest respect for a very large number of civil servants in all ranks. Nevertheless, I think I am correct in
believing-though I hope I am wrong, and that the minister will tell me if I am-there is no person with power and authority and responsibility to deal with the larger matters where millions and tens of millions of dollars are involved, and to come to a conclusion with an independent outside view whether this, that or the other department has enough people or too many. That should not be left to persons inside the department, or to an overworked finance department if it is in the authority of the Department of Finance. It seems to me, as I ventured to say once before, that we are in much the position the navy would be in if you put up a lot of admirals to try to reduce the navy: you would not get very far. You do not take admirals, you take somebody else. Economy, though the word is a tiresome one, is important. It is a pity there are so few people here to-day to consider this matter. In the small scope which the minister has described it sounds as if a fair job is being done. But I may interject this, that when the question of furniture came up under the Department of Public Works, the Minister of Public Works did not leave us with the impression that it had been dealt with necessarily in the most efficient manner. There were doubts left, even doubts expressed on the other side of the house.
I would put forward one point which I think is very important: have we any authority with independence and power to look in a detached way at these expenditures of hundreds of millions of dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
As the hon. member
realizes, when this division was set up it was for a specific purpose. As I have said, it was to review requisitions for printing, stationery, office equipment and furniture. Of course the biggest item of furniture that we have to deal with is filing cabinets.
I am satisfied with the answer the minister made as to the scope of this authority. I do not want to press that further. I want to know if the broader situation is dealt with.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: I do not know that I can answer that question. I do know that it has been given considerable study. I understand what the hon. member has in mind is someone in the capacity, say, of an overall purchasing agent, to see if the purchases of the various departments cannot be interrelated and coordinated.

It is something far beyond the matter of

Supply-Short Wave Broadcasting
purchase; it is the whole set-up of the business of the Dominion of Canada with 150,000 people carrying it on. It is a tremendous operation, where right scrutiny and decision might result in savings, not of a few hundred thousands, but of tens and tens of millions. That is what we are considering, and I am sure we should all have it deeply at heart. If not, we certainly do not express the views of the ordinary citizen of Canada in this matter, because they have it in mind in no uncertain way.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
I might say that the government has, too.
Mr. MACDOXNEI.L (Muskoka-Ontario): So far as I am concerned, the answer which the minister has given indicates that nothing adequate is being done to deal with the question of economies in a broad way.
