This, I understand, is an item for the operation of the short-wave station at Sackville. I am not opposing the item, because I think the short-wave station is an asset to Canada. But this vote with No. 258 and another supplementary item, amounts to approximately $1,500,000. One and a half million dollars is a lot of money to provide in one year for the operation of a short-wave broadcasting station from which we get no commercial return, or very little, and I should like to know whether this is to become an annual expenditure. I do not know anything about the technical end of radio, but it seems to me that $1,500,000 is a lot of money for maintenance and operation of a short-wave station for one year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
I agree that a million and a half dollars is a lot of money for the administration of a short-wave station. I am afraid that it is going to continue to cost a lot of money from year to year. It was the general opinion of the house, and the matter was brought before the radio committee of 1942 and of previous years, that a short-wave station should be established. That was done. The capital expenditure was enormous. The position of the C.B.C. with reference to it is that they carry it on. The expenses are voted and will continue to be voted yearly by parliament for that purpose.
I can give the hon. gentleman something of a breakdown of the service and what it costs. The items of expenditures are as follows: Performers-these are the people who broadcast and make up the programmes, $475,000; sal-

aries, $335,000. We pay $40,000 a year for a news service. That goes to the news agencies of Canada. Publicity costs us $25,000. We pay $12,000 a year for transmission lines. General operating overhead is $124,000. Rental of facilities in connection with that costs us $35,000. Power costs us $30,000 a year; tubes and maintenance, $31,000. Crescent street Sackville line, $42,000 a year. We have made improvements to the properties that we have leased, for which we pay rentals of $25,000. Supervision charges cost us $58,000. That makes up the total of $1,232,700. The capital expenditure for this year is $75,000. It was estimated that for improvements to grounds, dikes, roads, new structures, technical plant and antennae, an amount of $125,000 will be required. Fifty thousand dollars was voted for the fiscal year 1945-46, but has not yet been expended because it was not possible to find materials and contractors to undertake the various jobs. This $50,000 is included in the supplementary vote for 1946-47. The major item in the new capital cost is 21 megacycle antenna, costing some $55,000, which will be required owing to conditions which are the result of sun spots.
I might perhaps give a little information which would be of some benefit to the committee. At the present time the international service schedule approximates a peacetime pattern and broadcasts forty-seven hours a week to Europe, an hour a day to the West Indies. Then there is a test transmission of one and a half hours per week to Latin America. In the European service twelve hours a week are devoted to programmes provided for the Canadian forces who are still overseas. This particular service will terminate this fall. The rest of the forty-seven hours is made up of daily programmes to the United Kingdom, France, Czechoslovakia and Germany.
The European service is being extended to include programmes to Norway, Sweden, Denmark Belgium and Russia. Plans also call for a daily service to Latin America, New Zealand, Australia and South Africa. This proposed service will total 121^ broadcast hours per week. Because of the vastly greater audiences obtainable, the C.B.C. international service is making every effort to develop a relay system of broadcasting. A weekly programme from Canada has been relayed over one of the biggest stations in Rio de Janeiro since February. Other Canadian programmes have also been broadcast over local stations in that city. This fall a regular half hour programme to France will be inaugurated and will be carried on that country's national network. The B.B.C. are showing increasing

Supply-Short Wave Broadcasting
interest in Canadian programmes, and several regular series of relays have been arranged and are under discussion. Our West Indies programmes have been rebroadcast widely throughout the Caribbean.
The international service will concentrate on those countries in which Canada is particularly interested. While the programme budget will not permit of many expensive feature programmes, the C.B.C. believes that by exercising ingenuity and imagination, and with the help of the domestic service of the C.B.C., the funds requested will make possible a comparatively modest but nonetheless effective job of advertising Canada.
There were two purposes for which the international short-wave system was set up. First was the matter of urgency. It was emphasized that we should have a short wave means of communicating with our troops who were overseas. The job was finished in sufficient time to be of great use not only in bringing news to our armed services who were in different parts of the European continent, but in spreading propaganda to the people who were our allies over there, and even propaganda to our enemies. In addition to that it has the commercial feature that it will keep Canada before the different nations of the world. This is not a revenue-producing service at all. It was built primarily for the purpose which I indicated and with the object in view that we should keep the name of Canada before the rest of the world and advertise Canada to our potential customers, as well as the products and the other things that we had for sale.
Just to follow that up for a moment, I would express the hope that the short wave station does not carry the soap operas across the sea that we have to listen to in this country.

There is one thing that the minister forgot to say when he was speaking about the need of a high power short-wave station, namely, that a great many of us were disturbed in the early days of the war by the fact that the stations broadcasting in Great Britain would be bombed out.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: That is correct.

That was the real urgency in the matter. At that time I had correspondence from Great Britain along the lines which I have just mentioned. I mentioned it in the house and other members as well. One or two things disturb me about the maintenance of the short-wave station. Personally I think this station can be used to great advantage to Canada. Each department of government which uses the station should buy the time from the C.B.C. and put it in their own estimates instead of charging it up to the short-wave station. I do not think it is fair to have everything free over the short-wave system. I am not in favour of having a lot of this time free over this station.
The minister said that we have a news service which cost 840,000. I do not understand that. We are paying $70,000 to the Canadian Press for radio news. I think it is 840.000 to the United Press. I believe in that, but I do not see why we should have to pay another S40.000 for our short-wave station as well. I want to justify the expenditures on the short wave station. This station will be of great value in the future if it is properly handled and used, but it should not cost us nearly as much as it is costing to-day. If it were properly managed it should cost us much less than that.
The minister mentioned $35,000 for rent. What premises have the C.B.C. rented for the short wave system?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: This item is covered by order in council of September 1, 1944. It is rental payable for the use of studios and equipment provided by the C.B.C. in Montreal, Crescent street. The international service, which is separate entirely from the domestic service, pays a rental to the domestic service for that part which is used for international purposes. The same obtains with reference to the news service. We do pay $90,000 a year for the domestic service and $40,000 for the international, the two amounting to $130,000. It does not make much difference whether you pay the $130,000 all to the one source and charge the $40,000 to this, or make it two separate items, because the same people in the main are supplying the news, the Canadian Press, the Associated Press and the news service.
Does that mean that the premises and headquarters of the short-wave system are in Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: No. The short-wave station is at Sackville, but you have your people who are administering it and your programmes originating not where the station is located. That is why you have to have expensive wire service from the place of production of the programmes to the station which transmits them.

What I was trying to ascertain was the wisdom of setting up in Montreal what is virtually the chief premises of the short-wave system, whose station is at

Supply-Short Wave Broadcasting
Sackville when the C.B.C. headquarters are at Ottawa. What is the sense of going to Montreal? Would it not have been better to have them all together at Ottawa where the C.B.C. is situated?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: The hon. member will appreciate the difficulty. From the administrative end, it does not make so much difference where you have your offices, but from the point of view of producing programmes you could not possibly have your programme, studios and facilities where your short wave station is, because you have no big area there, nor have you the people to call upon to produce the programmes. So that we try to get that talent in metropolitan areas like Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg and Vancouver, where the talent is available. As regards Montreal, the reason is that that city is closest to the large production centres of the short-wave station.

I do not want to see the C.B.C. charged, so far as short-wave operations are concerned, with a lot of expenditures which should not really be charged to them on their overseas broadcasting account. You have to have broadcasting in different languages, but you do not have to translate music, and you have wires there too. You also have your press service, and it should not be charged to the overseas broadcasting all the time. That is going to be the tendency if we do not look out. We shall have the operations in Canada charged against the short-wave broadcasting overseas.

Is any revenue received at the moment from the short wave through advertising or otherwise, or is the policy against it? Is it anticipated in the future that there will be substantial revenue, or will it be entirely a voluntary service?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: There is no revenue at all from the operation, and it is not contemplated that there is likely to be a revenue, because it is not used by individual commercial people or firms. There are no countries that have commercial short-wave stations.
I take it that the station at Sackville is the only short-wave operated by the C.B.C. in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Yes.
How many days a week are they on the air, and how many hours a day?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: The short-wave station is on the air every day in the week. At the present time they are operating 47 hours a week, and we propose shortly to increase that output 121 hours.
What is the policy of the C.B.C. regarding the insurance of the plant, towers, aerials and other equipment belonging to the C.B.C. at Sackville?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: The item last year for insurance was $1,402.

Is that the amount of
premiums?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Yes.

What is the policy in the placing of this insurance? For some years I have been endeavouring to get the C.B.C. to place their insurance with maritime insurance firms. Finally after a good deal of correspondence and conversation with different ministers in charge of the work I got a letter, as far back as May 24, 1945, from the present minister. It is not marked as confidential, and I believe

Supply -Short Wave Broadcasting
I may be permitted to read it. I do this so that hon. members, and the people of Canada generally, will know the policy:
I wish to acknowledge the receipt of your communication of Hay 7 with reference to insurance on broadcasting station Sackville, N.B. It is your desire, I understand, that some of that insurance be given to a local firm.
I have taken the matter up officially with the general manager and chairman of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It appears that the corporation have a definite policy with reference to the placing of their insurance. They have an expert who advises on the amount and the type of insurance to be placed on any plant, and they have found it most beneficial and economical that that business be placed with one large firm.
I say the department could still retain the expert, still get advice from him and still try to give some of those in the maritime provinces who are in the insurance business a chance to secure some of this business. Matters connected with price, and responsibility of insurance companies, could all be considered. But it does not appear right to me, and to those who have been talking to me, that this business should be centralized. There is too much of this centralization to suit some of us in the maritime provinces.
This is one place where the government can show the way. It is true they cannot tell private enterprise where they are going to set up business, but they can give a lead. If the government can show hon. members why it is better to place this business with one large firm, situated probably in Montreal or Toronto, I should like to hear it, and I know the people of Canada would, too.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: I have nothing to add to what was said in the letter. That is the policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I do not make their policy. For business reasons they have established that policy and are carrying it out.
I should like to place one further point on the record. This is not a C.B.C. station.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Not at all.

It is a government-owned short-wave station recommended by a parliamentary committee, the recommendation being adopted by the House of Commons and put into operation so as to give Canada a voice in the affairs of the world. The C.B.C. operates only as agent of the government, does not own the station, and does not charge the people of Canada out of revenues received for any service rendered in connection with this short-wave station.

Since the hon. member for Cariboo has referred to some of my remarks, may I tell him that I am willing to accept this vote for chicken feed. As I said, I am not seriously objecting to it. However, I do want people to get the picture I have in mind which I believe is the true one. The hon. member has said that when a private broadcasting station operates it does cost the people something because advertising is charged in the price of goods. He says that does not fool anybody. The fact of the matter is that it has fooled him. That is not what happens at all. While that amount may be charged in the price of the goods, by reason of the advertising the manufacturer is able to sell in such volume that as a result the price of the goods to the consumer is reduced. If they did not have this advertising, the price of the goods would be higher because the manufacturer could not produce the goods in sufficient volume to put them on the market at an attractive price. So there are a few people who are not being fooled.

The hon. member has revealed how he has been fooled, in the last analysis, to assume that people do not know what they want unless they hear it blared at them ten or fifteen times a day. Such an assumption is ridiculous. I can get my soap without anyone telling me what kind I must get.

Item agreed to.
Supply-Broadcasting-Loans

Loans and investments: Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-
965. Loans to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation repayable with interest at a rate to be fixed by the governor in council on such terms and conditions as the governor in council may determine and to be applied in payment of expenditures on the construction, extension or improvement of capital works of the broadcasting facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in Canada. Such loans, with interest, shall be a charge on the revenues of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation next after the charge imposed under the provisions of section 17 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936, $2,000,-
000.

This is an interesting vote. Already we have had before the house a bill dealing with these matters; now we have something different. We have what I would call a subterfuge bill. It is just the same thing, but they are trying to make it smell a little sweeter by introducing it in this way. I do not wish to discuss the matter at length, but I should like to make some brief observations before this large amount of money is voted. This is your money, mine and everybody else's. It is the taxpayer's money. Before it is voted there should be more investigation of activities ,of this kind. The private corporations are willing to spend their own money to do a job which we are asking the taxpayers of Canada to put up the money for. These private corporations are also paying taxes into the treasury of Canada. We have no more need for another high-powered radio station in Canada than a cow has for a fifth foot. We are getting service there at the present time. Let the private stations do the job. Make them go up to their full power if you like, but do not spend the taxpayers' money.
It is all very well to say that we are going to have two voices in Canada, that we are going to have the trans-Canada network and the dominion network. The first thing you know we shall be spending more and more money. Let us have one really good network operated by the national corporation, and let us have another good network operated by the private stations. We shall then have two voices, and an opportunity to have two opinions. I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Macleod:
That vote No. 965, for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, be reduced to one dollar.
Mr. Chairman-
Question.
May I say to the hon. gentlemen who are crying "question" that they are a little previous.
Question.
No matter how much they cry it will not prevent one from saying what he wants to say about the expenditure of money.
You have said it already.
I have not said nearly enough. If my hon. friends want to go out in the lobby and smoke-
Or sleep.
-or go out to lunch or go to sleep, I do not care, but I am going to take up a little time to discuss a few things. This is an important item.
Question.

The hon. member who is making so much noise was on the radio committee and he should know the importance of this item. It is not merely the voting of $2,000,000; we are voting on a vital principle. If my French Canadian friends, whom I-
No.
Easy on that.
-admire for their stand-
Go ahead.

There is such a mass of hysteria over there that I do not quite understand it. I admire them for their stand on Canadianism; I am for them, but I say to them that I am pleading now for the preservation of that same Canadianism. It will pay them to hear what I have to say. Perhaps this speech should be coming from that corner of the house instead of here.
As I say, there is a vital principle involved. This tremendous organization has within it inherent and potential powers, unlimited powers, almost unthinkable powers. We have an organization here which can reach the ears of a quarter of a million people almost any time in the day. Tell me if that is not a powerful organization, a powerful medium for the dissemination of information and propaganda.
During the sittings of the radio committee there was presented a brief on behalf of the Canadian Association for Adult Education. I am not criticizing that association for one moment. I believe in education; a man is a fool not to believe in education. But there is a sense in which our educators can be wrong. They have not always been right, as history will prove. As I say, this organization came to the committee urging that the present radio set-up in Canada be maintained, in other words that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation

Supply-Broadcasting-Loans
be not interfered with in respect to their authoritarian powers and their control of radio in Canada. I have no criticism to make of their advancing that argument, because it is the right of any man or any organization to come before such a committee to make his or their desires known.
In the course of the hearings on their brief I brought out the fact that I had received a number of telegrams and letters from several farm forums in my constituency and others, organizations affiliated with the Canadian Association for Adult Education, which put out over the C.B.C. networks various talks on farm problems. I am not criticizing those programmes because I think some of them are very good. What I am criticizing is the fact that these farm forums were circularized by Canadian Association for Adult Education. They were asked to send in resolutions supporting the present radio policy in Canada, supporting the present status of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. One might say they had the right to do that. I am not questioning their right to do it, but an incident arose in the radio committee to which I should like to direct attention. I desired to bring this before the committee but the circumstances were such that I agreed to leave it over until the bill was presented. Now we have the estimate. The incident was simply this. I brought out the fact that many of these farm forums which were sending out these resolutions were doing so without a full knowledge of the facts. I did use the expression that in one case these people did not know beans about radio, and of course that was put over the news wires. I am not objecting to that.

You should not. You
said it.
It was your constituents who were objecting.
And you said it.
Certainly I said it.
Then why back up?
Their judgment may be just as good as yours.

I am not saying that
there are not a good many people in the country who do know what it means but I am saying on the basis of the circularization of those petitions that people responded because they enjoyed the farm forum programme, not because they knew all that was involved in the future of radio.
Now I am coming to the point I want to bring to the attention of the committee. I asked in the radio committee if the Canadian Association for Adult Education might have circularized their organizations, and I got the answer: Yes, it was quite possible they had. I shall not take time to turn up the page of the evidence, but I was led to believe that a certain resolution was sent out, which resolution was all right. I am not criticizing the resolution that was passed by the Canadian Association for Adult Education, but what I do criticize is a letter that was sent out to the farm forums and was never brought to the attention of the radio committee. I want to read that letter now. The secretary of the farm forums is a gentleman by the name of Ralph S. Staples. Mr. Staples presented a brief to the committee as representative of the union of cooperatives in Canada. I have no objection to that, and no objection to the brief that he presented. But in the brief he claimed that those who were opposing the taxation of cooperatives were able to pay for broadcasts, while evidently the cooperatives could not get the same service in putting their arguments before the people. I have no particular objection to that, but this Mr. Staples is the man who sent out this circular letter to the farm forums. I am going to read the letter, and I will ask my friends over there on the Liberal side of the house how they like it. The letter is dated Toronto, June 19, addressed to the secretaries of farm forums in Canada and headed, "An Important Message". It reads:
National Farm Radio Forum could not exist without the tremendous contribution made to the project by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. As you know the C.B.C. produces the broadcast and provides the time on the air, including the network facilities and so on. The C.B.C. does this as a service to the people of Canada, a service which does not cost farm forum or the other organizations which sponsor farm forum a single dollar.
Supply-Broadcasting-Loans
That is right.

Some gentleman, says
"That is right". That depends on the kind of glasses you are wearing. While it is true that farm forum is not a direct charge on the Canadian listening public, it is also true that the Canadian public are providing the networks and are paying four or five million dollars in licence fees to keep the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation going, thereby enabling the corporation to put over the programme known as farm forum. That is point No. 1 that should be made clear in the first paragraph of this letter. The second paragraph reads:
The national executive on farm radio forum meeting here yesterday expressed great concern because the C.B.C. is at the moment under heavy attack. The attack comes mainly from two sources:	(1) the private radio stations
through their organization, the National Association of Broadcasters, and (2) from the newspapers in Canada, many of which seem to regard radio as a competitor and some of which are controlled by interests financially involved in radio stations. The reasons for the attacks are not far to seek. Some of the larger private stations are making huge profits out of broadcasting and hope to make more if they are permitted to operate a network for profit. It is apparent that there are in this country interests which act as though they would like to choke off free discussion.
I want the members of this house to analyse that paragraph, and believe me, you cannot analyse it with any degree of intelligence without coming to the conclusion that a socialist wrote it.
What a pipe dream!
Suppose he did.

What is the situation? In the first place, where is the heavy attack coming from against the C.B.C. by press and radio? Apart from one or two editorials, which it is the freedom of the press to write, I do not believe the attack has been heavy at all-not nearly as heavy as I should have liked to see it. As for private radio making any attack on the C.B.C., the shoe is on the other foot. In the evidence submitted it was said that the most cordial relations existed between private stations and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. My criticism is of that sort of letter going out individually to farm forum organizations asking them to back the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in their present status. I am not saying that they have no right to be asked to do it; I am criticizing that kind of letter.
The third paragraph reads:
As is done at frequent intervals, the House of Commons has appointed a committee to make a study of radio broadcasting and to bring in

recommendations. This committee represents all parties. There are twenty-five members of the committee. The national executive of farm radio forum feels that the forum should support those members of this parliamentary committee who contend that radio broadcasting in Canada should continue to be carried on primarily as a service to the people of Canada and not necessarily for the money ivhich can be made.
Now, analyse that paragraph, and I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that that is one of the most insidious reflections upon certain members of the radio committee. Let me read it again:
The national executive of farm radio forum feels that the forum should support those members of this parliamentary committee who contend that radio broadcasting in Canada should continue to be carried on-
He does not say, by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
-primarily as a service to the people of Canada and not necessarily for the money which may be made.
What is wrong with that?
There is a lot wrong with that.
Explain.
My friend wants it explained. I was going to say, any stupid muttonhead could read the meaning of that paragraph.
Otherwise you would never have got it, would you?
The letter was sent to these farm forums; it was not sent to me.
And to the hon. member for Cariboo.

It is saying that there is a section of members of the radio committee that are there for the specific purpose of seeing that radio is run-so that men can make money out of it instead of giving service to the people of Canada. I repudiate and refute that.
He does not say it is you.
He says, certain members of the committee.
You are not all those members.
Well, of course I am only one, but the intention of the paragraph is as plain as anything can be.
Absolutely.

I say that every member of that radio committee was interested only

Supply-Broadcasting-Loans
in giving the best possible radio service to Canada, and at all times, commensurate with it, of preserving our glorious heritage of free institutions. Every last member of the committee -had that in mind, and that only.
I support the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I speak to service clubs, and I have spoken on the subject of radio in Canada and plugged for the C.B.C. Now, believe it.
We do.

Here is another paragraph:
A dangerous proposal has been made-
Who said it was dangerous?
A dangerous proposal has been made, namely that the broadcasting act should be amended in such a way as to remove from the board of governors of "the C.B.C. the authority necessary to regulate radio broadcasting in Canada.
Here is a man who, with the .Canadian radio networks at his disposal, takes it upon himself to circularize the people saying that a proposal which might be made to have a separate regulatory body that will be perfectly neutr-al is a very dangerous proposal. Let me go on:
It is unnecessary to set forth what the results of such a change might easily be.
There is an insidious sentence of inference, the writer knowing full well that the people lo whom he addresses the letter are not cognizant of all the facts. And that is the thing I object to. Here is the last paragraph:
If you value a radio system that is not controlled by wealth-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. It is one
o'clock.
Very well, Mr. Chairman. I thought may be I might finish the one paragraph.

Finish the paragraph.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I move, Mr. Chairman, that you report the resolutions and ask leave to sit again this day.
The hon. gentleman had just a few lines in the paragraph to put on the record to complete what he had to say, and I think it would be well if he were allowed to do that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Probably it would be better if the hon. member completed the paragraph.

I will just read this part:
If you value a radio system that is not controlled by wealth then we urge you to get in touch with your member of parliament at Ottawa by wire just as soon as you can.
As to that, Mr. Chairman, let me say that if you can prove to me that a socialist did not write that sentence, then-
Come off that! It makes no difference what a man's political views are when he writes a letter for an organization; and I don't know what he is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the paragraph completed?

No. It continues:
A very short wire will do. All you need to indicate is that you like the C.B.C. and that you support it in its present form.
You might think he was writing to some school boys.
You should sign it as secretary of your farm forum. A copy of the wire should be mailed to Mr. Ralph Maybank, M.P., chairman of the special committee on radio broadcasting, House of Commons, Ottawa.
In matters of this nature the farm radio forums across Canada can have an influence far greater than their numbers would indicate.
Yours sincerely.

Believe me, they did it.
Progress reported.
Resolutions reported.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I wish to move that these resolutions be read the second time and concurred in, so that they may be put in print immediately for the preparation of the bill which will be based on them.

Before we go on with this, I am not at all certain of the procedure which is being followed, but I understand that we are not concurring in any resolution at this stage if it has to do with the matter now under discussion.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No. That resolution has not been passed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The resolution which was under consideration by the committee when the committee rose has not been reported.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I move:
That the resolutions considered in committee of supply this day and reported be read the second time and concurred in.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: The house having reverted to motions:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND AUSTRALIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to table copy of an agreement between Canada and Australia for air services between the two countries, signed in Ottawa, June 11, 1946, and effective of that date. I may say that simultaneous announcement is being made in Canberra and Ottawa on this day. I have a statement with regard to the air line which, if it is agreeable to hon. members, I will have printed in Hansard, to save time.

subtopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND AUSTRALIA
speechtext: On the understanding, Mr. Speaker, that after it is printed hon. members may ask any questions which may arise with respect to it, as is normally done when a statement is made in the house.

subtopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND AUSTRALIA
speechtext: Quite.

Canada has already signed bilateral agreements with the United States, United Kingdom and Newfoundland. The present agreement with Australia represents the fourth in a series which we shall be negotiating to open the way for the Canadian international air services we plan to operate in accordance with information I have on previous occasions given to this house.
The agreement with Australia follows the standard pattern of our other bilateral agreements,-a pattern which was approved for general international use at the Chicago conference on international civil aviation in 1944. It provides for an exchange of traffic rights between Canada and Australia so that an air line designated by the government of Australia may put down and take up at Vancouver passengers, mail and cargo from Australia, while an airline designated by the government of Canada, which will be Trans-Canada Air Lines, may put down and take up in Australia traffic to and from Canada. The route to be followed by the airline designated by Australia is via Fiji, Canton Island, Honolulu and San Francisco. The route to be followed by Trans-Canada Ajr Lines is not yet finally decided and accordingly is not specified in the agreement.
It is understood that the airline to be designated by Australia will be a joint company owned and operated by the governments of rMr. St. Laurent.]
Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom. In order that arrangements may be completed for the Pacific route this will, of course, involve a further civil aviation agreement between Canada and New Zealand as well, and discussions to this end have already been initiated.
In order to provide for complete cooperation on the Pacific run, between Trans-Canada Air Lines and the joint Australia-New Zealand-United Kingdom airline, a special clause has been added in the annex to the agreement looking to a pooling arrangement between the two air lines and a reciprocal exchange between them of traffic rights enjoyed by each along the route. This complete and full cooperation will be in accordance with plans originally worked out at the commonwealth discussions on civil aviation held in Montreal in the autumn of 1944.
I am not at the moment able to give the house complete information as to when we may initiate our trans-Pacific air service. This will depend upon a number of factors such as the conclusion of other necessary bilateral agreements along the route and the availability of suitable equipment and facilities. It is my expectation, however, that the year 1947 may see Canadian planes making regular scheduled runs to the southern Pacific.

I contend that there was no need for the letter, and certainly there was no need to imply that there was any such danger as was implied. Even if there were set up another network in Canada under the management of private radio, it would not render the corporation one bit less effective in the service that they are able to give to the country. The farm forum programmes would go over the air just the same, and so would the other educational features sponsored by the C.B.C. I am not implying that we have to do away with the corporation just because some of us are recommending that there be a neutral regulatory body. It appears to me that the whole scheme and process of preventing that from happening is to strike fear into the minds of some people wrho are enjoying certain programmes, and by implication lead them to believe that radio service in this respect is to be curtailed.
I should like to ask the minister whether or not it would be possible to place on the record the names of the secretaries of the various farm forums. I should like for a moment or two to pursue another aspect of the matter and attempt to show the potential dangers which are inherent in the authoritarian powers now held by the corporation. When I was speaking on the first reading of the bill which was introduced the other day I likened the corporation to the possibility of a newspaper corporation under government ownership, should one be established. I tried to give an illustration to show that if the same thing were happening in newspaper enterprise which is happening to-day in radio, the people of the country would be seriously alarmed. I drew that illustration, but I want to go one step further. I did not have time to develop this particular point the other night, but it is well known, and we can put it down as basic, that radio is still in its infancy. It is a rapidly growing science, and there is now appearing in the field of radio a science known as facsimile. Hon. members of the committee are aware of just what it is, but should some who might occasionally read Hansard wonder what the term means may I explain that facsimile is a process of transmitting by the air waves over the radio the printed page. That branch of radio science is already an accomplished fact. It is true that in this development we in Canada have not gone so far, but two newspapers in the United States are, I understand, already giving that service. One of them is giving it as a service, and the other is in the experimental stage. The facsimile process simply means that one can tune in his radio, get the news as he does now, and at the same time the news is printed right there and then in front of him. After he has heard it he can go to his set and tear off the sheet just as you would tear a sheet of paper off a roll of wrapping paper, and there in front of his eyes is the record on the printed page. Not only is that an accomplished
fact but it may be only four or five years before the same thing can be done in pictures in three or four colours. The point I am trying to make is that not only are the potential powers now inherent in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation going to drive private radio out of business, but I sound the alarm that by the method of facsimile they are going to drive the press out of business. Someone will say you cannot arrest the progress of science. No. You certainly cannot, but the point I want to put before the committee is that facsimile is done by radio process, and there is now inherent in the present broadcasting act all the powers of the present radio corporation to control radio. You do not need to give them one iota more power to control facsimile.
Perhaps we do not need to be greatly excited if the press of Canada should sound an alarm at the growing powers of C.B.C.; neither can we afford to be too much excited when some of us suggest that there be a neutral body with regulatory powers and that these powers be removed from the corporation. It would not diminish in any way the service which the corporation gives the country. I sound that alarm because that is something that is coming. Make no mistake about it. It is not very far off.
I would make as a further argument that because we are still in the infancy of radio, together with the growing part of radio known as frequency modulation and the other aspect known as facsimile, and so forth, the C.B.C. would be far better off financially and otherwise not to take over these channels at the present time, but to bide a wee and let the thing rest for a couple of years or so. Let them tell these private stations CFRB and CFCN that they must step up their power to 50 watts. My information is that they are prepared to do it. We know by the record that they have repeatedly asked permission to do it, and I am suggesting that they be given that permission and thus the 50 kilowatt channels will be reserved for Canada. Freedom of speech means this, that if one man gets on the air, or anywhere else, another person has a perfect right to answer him. If he has not that right, then we have not free speech. That is the position. I realize that where there are several millions of people in a nation we cannot have each of them saying, "I want to answer the commentator who was on the air last night." I know that would be physically impossible. But let us not accentuate the idea that the C.B.C. are the guardians of free speech because they say they want all shades of public opinion to be expressed. Free speech is free only when everybody has an opportunity to present his case.
I have two suggestions to make. The first is that they do away altogether with commentators. I do not think they are needed. But I am not offering that suggestion without making an alternative suggestion. In their place they should have weekly round-table discussions on the most recent topic, to be conducted by three or four speakers who would have directly opposite views. The discussions should be entirely unrehearsed. By this means the people could be told all about the particular subject. I would guarantee that such a programme would have one of the largest listening audiences in Canada. Often I listen to the town hall meeting of the air in the United States. That programme has prominent men taking part, government officials, heads of labour organizations and even governors of states. It is unrehearsed and is an extremely interesting programme. They stop at nothing-I suppose common sense would prevent a man swearing at another- in discussing the latest topic, whether it is politically hot, international or whatever it is.
I have a further suggestion to make. If the corporation is still bent on keeping this handful of commentators on the air, I suggest that no one commentator be allowed to stay on the programme for more than one or two months at the most, and then he should be heard no more for at least a few years. Surely there are enough well-informed men in Canada that we do not have to filter all this information through a dozen half pints of brain. Surely there are enough capable people in Canada to keep this thing going indefinitely. Now, to have the mere statement made that there ought to be a neutral court at this time, and immediately to accept it without again going into all the principles that underlay the legislation in 1932 and 1936, seems to me to be precipitate action, and as far as I am concerned I am confident I can keep an open mind upon the question until we can give it full consideration.

Now I come to this question of expansion which has been mentioned and which is all that is called for at the present moment by the $2,000,000 vote. The expansion of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has been envisaged every year since 1936. It was part of the original plan; it was examined year by year from that time onward. Such expansion as could take place up to 1939 was necessarily interrupted by the war. Committees from time to time, unanimously I believe, have recommended that this expansion should go forward, and it is in this year that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation comes to the point where it can carry out the dictates of former committees and of parliament. That is our starting point this year. The expansion of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation calls for the operation of certain stations which are at present being operated by private broadcasters. It does not call for the corporation taking over the stations; it calls for them operating upon certain wave lengths. Canada was granted a certain number of clear channel wave lengths. This was done by the Havana treaty, an international treaty, which assigned these wave lengths to us. It is understood that they must be operated at 50,000 watt power. They are as follows: CKY at Winnipeg, CFCN at Calgary and CFRB at Toronto. It is not necessary that Canada herself should develop these channels up to 50,000 watts; it could be done by a private owner so far as international law and treaty are concerned. But if we are to have these clear channels it is necessary that they be developed.
We find ourselves in this position. We have to decide whether we shall allow some private owner to develop these channels up to 50,000 watts, or whether we shall do it ourselves under the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. When we obtained the channels it was intended that they would be developed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. That has been known by parliament from that day to this. The measure has been endorsed whenever opportunity arose to endorse it. Moreover, all persons who have private stations have them clearly upon the understanding all these years that the amount of power allowed to them was the same as would be allowed to every other owner of a private station. They have clearly understood that no private station would be singled out and allowed to raise its power up to 50,000 watts. If we were to grant to the present owners of CFRB, CFCN and CKY the right to raise their power up to 50,000 watts we would be rankly and grossly discriminating in favour of them as against all other private 63260-355J

It would not be feasible for any organization to attempt to exist only on indirect advertising. Indirect advertising is of the sort where a programme is put on the air and an announcer says, "This is brought to you with the compliments of such and such corporation." That ends the advertising and then follows the symphony or whatever the programme may be.
As every person knows, direct advertising is advertising which may occur right in the middle of a programme, and it generally. occurs at the beginning and end. It takes the form of "Buy Camel cigarettes," or "Use Lifebuoy soap," and so on. We listen to hockey broadcasts which tell us about Imperial Oil. As I said, advertising methods have changed, and I do not see how C.B.C. or any other organization could continue to exist without that type of advertising. I mentioned Fibber McGee a little earlier. That programme could not go on a network if only indirect advertising was permitted, nor could we have these hockey broadcasts, because they are direct advertising.

Mr. Chairman, unquestionably the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, the chairman of the radio committee, has made an excellent speech. He has placed before this committee the case of the C.B.C., and has given the reasons and arguments which have been put forward in order that Bill 391 may come to be. On the other hand I cannot help but feel that his arguments are as hollow as a drum, and I want to beat upon that drum for a few minutes. I do not for a moment wish to attempt to discredit his arguments from the point of view of the sincerity with which they have been put forward, first by the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and now by the chairman of the radio committee. Nor do I wish to take up one by one these arguments. I will make my own speech in my own way, which I hope will cover, for the information of the members, the ideas I have in mind.
In the first place I should like to make my own position clear. For reasons sufficiently well known to the members of the house, and upon which it is not necessary for me to dwell, I have not been able to sit in this house until just recently. But I have been able to follow the deliberations of the house through Hansard and the reports of the various committees; therefore I have some knowledge of what took place in the radio

committee. From 1935 to 1940 I was a member of that committee, and I have been interested in radio since its very earliest beginning. In fact I personally broadcast over the air as early as 1922; I was on the air continuously from 1925 to 1939 and frequently since, and for two years in the 1930's I was interested in the radio advertising business, with which I have no connection whatever to-day. It so happens that some of my closest friends are in th radio business, either with C.B.C. or with private stations.
I want to make clear what my opinion of the C.B.C. is. I think the C.B.C. is an excellent organization for the purpose for which it was designed. But when it goes beyond that purpose I feel it is time for this house to check its progress along channels through which it was not designed to go. C.B.C. is a body possessed of as fine executive radio talent as there is in this country. I have nothing but the highest praise for men in the radio game such as Mr. Ernest Bushnell and Mr. Charles Jennings, to mention only two who are completely outstanding and have the respect of radio broadcasters in all countries. Their service and the service of the C.B.C. in many of its specialized functions is a credit to Canada and has done Canada good. I think therefore, speaking in those general terms, I have made myself clear as to what I think of the C.B.C. as it was designed to be. I should like to add this further word, that it has always been very kind and considerate to me in connection with matters in which I happened to be interested or with which I was connected.
I said a few moments ago, "the purpose for which it was designed." I think it would do no harm. Mr. Chairman, to take a few minutes of the committee's time to make clear the purpose for which C.B.C. was designed. That takes us back-I do not want to immerse the committee in a bath of history-to the inception of the Canadian Radio Commission, which later became the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. There was a situation prevailing in radio at that time -which was most involved and from the point of view of solution, most elusive. We were young in radio in Canada, while immediately next to us tens and later scores and then hundreds of millions of dollars were being spent by that mighty nation, the United States, whose programmes were infiltrating Canada. There was no particular policing of Canadian broadcasts. There were no particular regulations, except in a loose and general way, and there was a definite absence of service of Canadian programmes to all parts of Canada. This situation was thoroughly 63260-356
covered in the Aird report, which has been aired so often and so thoroughly. Hence it was felt desirable that there should be brought into being a regulatory body which in its turn would bring to all parts of Canada a Canadian radio service.
I was interested in the formation of the Canadian radio commission. I knew its chairman intimately, the late Hector Charles-worth, and I know whereof I speak. Hon. members may wish to draw out and expand and make deeper and put implications into the formation of the Canadian Radio Commission which later became the C.B.C., but I am telling this commitee the facts, and that is as far as the duties of the Canadian Radio Commission originally went. It was designed to control, to police and to censor. It was to be a regulatory body composed of those who knew something about radio broadcasting. It was to protect the radio listener from unfortunate Canadian programmes which might be aired from time to time, and it was to put Canada on the air map in so far as special services were concerned which were beyond the power or the pocket book of the Canadian advertiser. It was, then, to regulate and supervise. It was next to give programmes to all of Canada, and as my hon. friend who has just taken his seat has said, especially to the more remote parts of Canada not served by radio. So it was that in 1932 there were those in parts of Canada which are not so remote who could get no programmes whatever, let alone from the United States. It was to give to Canada an impartial news service, not sponsored by any newspaper, which news might conceivably be coloured by the opinions of that paper, but a Canadian news service. It was to report on world events from its correspondents throughout the world, correspondents in the pay originally of the commission and later of the corporation, just the same as to-day the British Broadcasting Corporation, the Columbia, and other networks have their correspondents in all parts of the world. It was to -bring reports of special events of wide interest. It was to bring to the listener, therefore, a specialized service. It was to canadianize its own programmes, divorced from advertising. It was to give a short-wave service to carry the voice of Canada to all parts of the world. It was to give educational programmes of a kind and type that no commercial sponsor would ever promote. It was therefore to raise radio out of merely the field of entertainment into the field of information and, shall I say, education.

I postulate, Mr. Chairman, that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as constituted to-day is virtually doing these very things. It may not be doing them as fully as is required by the listener; it may not be doing them as fully as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation themselves would like to do them, but within the limitations of the money at their disposal I consider the C.B.C. is doing an outstandingly good job. It can do better, and will. Then why this vote? Is this vote in order to employ more Canadian, talent in Canada? Is it to raise the basic scale of pay to Canadian artists? Is it for the purpose of giving better programmes? No, it is not. This vote is for the physical expansion of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. In the face of the fact that 94-7 per cent of Canada is at present covered-which is virtually saturation-the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation wishes to expand network programmes, and the expansion of network programmes means perforce under this vote that monopolistic control will be totally, completely and finally in the hands of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat has stated that the wave lengths provided under international agreement and at present in the possession of CFRB, Toronto, CFCN, Calgary, and CKY, Winnipeg, are wave lengths on which there must be broadcasting of a power of 50,000 watts. In spite of the fact that the possessors of those wave lengths have had them over a period of years and have given satisfactory service, as has been pointed out repeatedly, to the listeners in their community and within their range, they are not to be permitted to increase their power to the 50,000 watts because, were that permission granted, there would be discrimination against all other stations and discrimination in favour of them. That is the drum, Mr. Chairman, on which I am pounding. I think that is as hollow as a tympani. It is much better, therefore, in accordance with the arguments of my hon. friend, that these Canadian stations, giving a service to the people of Canada which-as has been pointed out too frequently for me to repeat-is a good service, should be put out of business. I asked the hon. gentleman if the facilities necessary for a privately owned network were made available to the private stations, could not the C.B.C. pick up the best of their programmes and air them through their own outlets? His answer was "Certainly." Well, then, why do we spend $2,000,000 of the taxpayers' money at this time when that can

be done and done successfully without it? Why not let the advertiser's dollar develop that network?
This history of radio broadcasting has proven beyond peradventure that government-owned, government-operated and government-developed broadcasting cannot possibly compete with private enterprise under the advertising sponsor.

I can support a vote for the betterment of the service of the C.B.C. This morning votes 257 and 258 for the increase of the facilities, the service and the maintenance of our shortwave station were before the committee. I heartily subscribed to it. If this vote of $2,000,000 were for the betterment of the service, for the employment of the finest news broadcasters who could be obtained as wandering reporters over the world for the C.B.C., I would vote for it, because that is the purpose of the C.B.C. Why should the end of private enterprise in broadcasting be brought about? I was about to deal with that point when the minister interrupted me a moment ago. I said that the purpose of this vote was to create a monopoly. Why should it be the end? I will tell him. Let me draw on my own experience in a practical way. He knows as well as I do that the success of any broadcasting station is based on the audience which it can acquire. The success of any newspaper is the extent of its circulation. Just as we have an audit bureau of circulation in the periodical and newspaper fields to study the circulation of a newspaper so that advertising rates may be based accordingly, so we have in radio. We have surveys. First it was comical the way they were done. Later on the methods were improved. To-day the chairman of the committee, the minister, the general manager of the broadcasting corporation or any one else can with great accuracy ascertain the audience of g,ny station.

Habits of listening change. Let hon. members remember this. In the old days it was fun to turn on one's radio, monkey around with the dials, and become what was known as a D-X hound. You would hear one programme for a few minutes, shift over to another and so on to see how many stations you could hear in an evening. Those days have gone. Then the listener went through the phase of picking out the programmes he liked on one station and the programmes he liked on another and in between times he did not bother keeping the radio on. To-day it is altogether different. The greatest proportion of radio listeners have their own favourite station and to that station they listen most of the broadcasting hours of the day. That station therefore has developed what is called its own audiences.
Let it be understood that in going out to sell their time to a would-be sponsor or advertiser these private stations can say that their audience is such and so, and they are right. On the other hand if you smother a station, if you blanket it, if you take away its traditional wave length and put it off in the cat-fight somewhere, the audience goes. And in the case of CFRB-let me speak of it-I know where it will go. It will go over to Buffalo, over to WKBW, WGRN and WBN. The C.B.C. is in competition with what the private station is able to offer without the ability to have a network. What the private station is able to offer is a local station. They cannot go out and sell time on a network. The surveys have shown that the C.B.C. cannot take competition. There are programmes of the C.B.C. which are listened to, as they should be; but throughout the day the C.B.C. has had to bend the knee to the private station even when that private station has not had the advantage of a network. Therefore I ask, do we want elimination of private broadcasting? Let there be no misunderstanding about it; if hon. members want the elimination of private broadcasting, vote for this item, which will accomplish that purpose.
I cannot overestimate the importance of radio. Sometimes I think it is possible for us, close as we are to the centre of things in Ottawa, to lull ourselves into a sense of misunderstanding. Radio is dynamite. It is not understood. Its power has had one dramatic manifestation in the course of the world's history. Had it not been for radio there would have been no world war II. Adolf Hitler would not have been possible. It was only through the magic of radio, that fantastic medium, that he was able to speak

Surely no member of the Liberal party is prepared to rise in his place in this house and say the C.B.C. ought to be the mouthpiece of any particular party. But it is; it is to the extent that it gives the Toronto Star free time. That fact was brought out clearly.
In 1943 the Canadian Press contracted to make its complete news report available to the national network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The price agreed upon was $40,000 per annum. The news was to be delivered, by wire to five C.B.C. regional offices from coast to coast, namely, Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver. The term of the contract was to be the duration of the war and six months thereafter.
At the same time the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation made a contract with the British United Press for the use of the B.U.P. foreign news report. The price to be paid was $25,000. In its other details this contract largely followed the one made by the C.B.C.

with the Canadian Press, except that the term of the contract was one year, automatically renewed unless certain agreed notice of cancellation was given by either side.
During 1944 the C.B.C. organized its second trans-Canada network, which became known as the dominion network. The corporation took the stand that it was unnecessary to make a separate purchase of news services for use on this new system. The contracts of both the Canadian Press and the British United Press were held to give the corporation the right to use the news delivered to it for any news purposes which the corporation might have and without restriction as to any specific network.
Shortly after the C.B.C. had thus established its right to use the news which it was receiving for its general purposes, it undertook on behalf of the government the operation of the short-wave broadcasting station at Sackville. Almost its first act of management was to purchase a news service for the use of the station. The contract was given to Canadian Press, not only without any competition, but also with the stipulation that no other news service was to be purchased. Remember, the short-wave station at Sackville was to use only one news service, and-let us be fair about it-that news service was veiy complimentary to the government. Although the news was only for use by this one station, without any transcontinental carriage or delivery at regional points involved, the price given to the Canadian Press was $45,000.
The contrast between what the C.B.C. was securing for its national and dominion networks combined for $40,000, and what it was spending $45,000 upon for the'single government-owned short-wave station is glaring. Quite obviously the corporation did not carry into its role as manager for the government the same financial thrift and close bargaining that it practised where its own finances were concerned.
During the past year, however, the C.B.C. agreed to increase its payment to the Canadian Press from $40,000 to $70,000 annually. This concession was made, regardless of the fact that, for purposes of government contracts, the end of the war has not yet been legally proclaimed. In other words, the contract ran to the end of the war and we have not yet legally reached the end of the war. So far as Canada is concerned, the war is not yet over, and yet C.B.C. changed its news contract and increased the price it was going to pay for it. These are the things we are worried about. We are concerned also about the power which we are giving to ministers of the crown and to the various bureaucratic organizations which they have created. The people of this country are finding that, no matter what move they make, what they do, what they say, they are responsible in some way or another to somebody who is an official of the government of Canada.
I can well remember back in 1917 and on to around 1930, at a time when everybody in the province of Ontario felt that he was under the eye of some spy, someone who was trying to find out whether he was violating the Ontario Temperance Act. I believe that one of the reasons which made the people of this province vote for the repeal of the Ontario Temperance Act was the fact that a spy system had been built up. We have done the same thing here. We have created organizations-the	Canadian Broadcasting
Corporation, for example, and the wartime prices and trade board-which have taken away from parliament the power to govern. Parliament has been deprived of its power to pass laws, to such an extent that it is a wonder to me how patient the people of Canada have been. We must be very careful before we continue along this course. I can readily understand why the C.C.F. party is supporting this bill, because it is just one more measure toward socialism, or communism-call it what you like. But those of us who believe in free enterprise, who hold that we have the right to live our own lives, to raise our children in freedom and enable them also to live their own lives, cannot possibly vote for such a measure as this.

If it were not that we had the C.B.C. to protect the interests of the Canadian people we would find ourselves with the whole medium of public education passing into the hands of private monopoly. My information in this regard is that the privately owned radio stations in the United States of America refused, up until a few years ago, to sell time to the cooperatives. At that time they were forced by the government to extend that privilege to all classes in the community.
I finish that point by saying that the hon. member for Macleod is quite right when he says that this is important. With the private stations it is only those who have money who can buy any time. In that event I am afraid that neither my hon. friend nor I shall ever be heard. I have never been and I do not know whether my hon. friend has, but certainly neither of our parties would ever be if we had to buy time. I am glad that this control is in the hands of the C.B.C., which makes it possible for us to get at least a little time along with the other philosophies in this country. When you are buying services of this kind on a private basis it means whatever the traffic will bear, and there are two things that happen. First, you rule out to a great degree the large masses of people from having its benefits and, second, inevitably you build up a privately owned monopoly. Those are two things that come from youi so-called free competition.
My hon. friend took a gratuitous slap at the People's Weekly, a paper which opposes the ideas for which he stands and referred to it as a funny paper. If my hon. friend found himself on the pages of a funny paper, then for the first time in his life he was where he ought to be. He went on to say that, when consulted, the people did not seem to understand about radio. I would say to him that
no doubt the people understand as much about radio as they did about social credit when the Social Credit party came to power. I do not like the inference in my hon. friend's argument that some body somewhere must tell the people what they must do with respect to a technical question like radio.
If that is true, who is to do it? Is it to be a private corporation, or is it to be a body responsible to parliament? If any body is to do it, then I say that the people who control parliament should do it. Frankly, I have more faith in the people than my hon. friend has. I think he reflects on their judgment with respect to both of us, because they sent us here. I hope they did not make a mistake in both cases, but it is quite within the realm of possibility that they did. They have the right to make that mistake if, indeed, they made it.
I want to follow up a little farther the other argument of my hon. friend. He speaks of the board as being authoritarian; he laid emphasis on the authoritarian phase of the thing. There is no such authoritarian idea in the board. My hon. friend is playing fast and loose with a certain sentiment which is a hangover of a great world conflict. He is trying to scare the people into his way of thinking by utilizing an idea that has been scaring people very badly ever since Hitler began to come to power. There are no such authoritarian powers. This parliament is supreme over anything that this government handles. If it is not, we should go home; we should not be here at all. If I thought parliament was not supreme I would not stay here for two minutes.
It is supreme now, despite the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite are Liberals and despite the fact that they do things with which I disagree most sharply. Still, what they do is what this parliament says they can do, because they represent the majority. Every four years the people of Canada, have the right to say who shall represent the majority. While that is true, it is not true for anyone to say that a board appointed by this government and responsible to this government is exercising authoritarian powers.
Then he said he would like to have a neutral body governing these things. Where would he find it? What does a neutral body mean? Neuter is one of the genders in grammar. There is feminine, masculine and neuter. Two are virile, and the other is lifeless, a thing without life or sex. That is neuter, and my hon. friend would have a body governing our radio commission which would be a sort of polyglot, hermaphrodite conglomeration of something that stands for nothing in par-

Not having been a member of the radio committee this year, and having had several other heavy responsibilities to discharge, I have had to depend in large measure on what I have heard on the floor of the house for an understanding of what this is about. I may say at the outset that the bill which the government presented was repugnant to me and, if that bill indicated the general policy that guides the CJB.C., I would say it is cause for considerable alarm throughout the country. However, perhaps it did not exactly represent the government's idea or that of the C.B.C. I should like to ask several pointed questions of the minister

and have his answers to them so that I may be able to form some accurate estimate of just what the C.B.C. is aiming at.
However, before I ask those questions, may I say that I have had great admiration for the C.B.C. ever since it began its activities. I have appreciated the high quality of programme that it has given the Canadian people. I have always felt that the C.B.C. had its place, just as I have felt that the private radio stations had theirs, and I have been of the view that the C.B.C. should keep its hands off private radio stations, leaving them to discharge their responsibility in the country. The evidence which has been presented before the house rather fills me with anxiety lest the C.B.C. is overstepping its bounds. I understand that when a private radio station receives its licence it is taken for granted that every year when it applies for a renewal of that licence it will receive that renewal on condition of good behaviour. I look upon the C.B.C., in reference to this parliament, in very much the same way. When the C.B.C. comes to parliament for grants of money to carry on each year I feel that it should look upon this as an application for the renewal of its licence, and I feel further that it should receive renewal of that licence on condition of good behaviour.
Some of the evidence which has come before us indicates that the C.B.C. has been trying to kick some of the private stations around. If that has occurred, then I believe the C.B.C. should be warned in the matter, advised to reform its ways in the future and given another chance.
In order to satisfy myself, I desire to ask a series of definite questions, for two purposes. First, they will give me an opportunity of learning things about the C.B.C. which I believe every member of the house ought to know and the country has a right to know. Then, it will give the government and the minister representing the C.B.C. a chance to set it right before the country. If there has been misrepresentation, such misrepresentation can be cleared away.
I am sorry I have not a copy of all these questions, but I have a copy of the first nine of them, and I shall send it to the minister so that he will be able to answer the questions one after the other. I should think he would not require a copy of the last ones in order to be able to answer them. I shall send the first ones to the minister, and shall proceed to ask the questions.
Is the government aiming to encourage the development of private radio stations in Canada? I take it, if that is the aim, then the C.B.C. must be aiming to do the same thing.

Otherwise I must assume that it is beginning to act as though it were a law unto itself. If that should be shown to be the case, then I would suggest that the situation is not as it should be.
Is the government endeavouring to give the Canadian people what they want over the radio, or is the government aiming to give what the government, through the C.B.C., wants the Canadian people to hear?
If the government is trying to give the Canadian people what the Canadian people want, what steps has the government taken to make sure that it is doing this?
Is the government aiming to establish and maintain freedom of speech in Canada over the radio?
If so, what steps has the government taken -and when I refer to the government I would presume that we would mean the C.B.C.-[DOT] to establish and maintain freedom of speech over the radio in Canada?
Does the government believe that the majority of the people in any given area of Canada-say a province, section of a province, an audience listening to a given local radio station-ought to be guaranteed the right to listen to any speaker or programme of the choice of those people in that area?
If so, what steps has the government or the C.B.C. taken to see that this state of affairs is brought about?
What in the minister's opinion ought to be the aim of radio in Canada?-entertainment, culture (literary, dramatic, or musical), education, enlightenment? If there are any others, the minister would be free to specify them.
Has the government provided adequate safeguards to prevent the C.B.C. from (a) impairing the strength and efficiency of private radio stations; (b) destroying the strength and efficiency of private radio stations; (c) destroying freedom of speech over private radio stations? What are the safeguards the government has taken in each of these respects?
From this series of questions dealing with the general attitude of the government and of the C.B.C. which, of course, would constitute their policy in Canada, I pass on to some details. The minister, I thought, resented the statement by the hon. member for Greenwood that, if this item were passed, it would ensure the destruction of private radio stations in Canada. I thought the minister was desirous of rising to refute that statement. I trust he will be able to make a good case in refutation of that charge.
